newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW-Indonesia's promise snags fund meeting.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-Indonesia's promise snags fund meeting.

text.p: The anticipated development of a huge domestic investor base in Indonesia, with its large population and bright economic promise, has generated the country's first mutual-fund conference.
"Mutual funds in Indonesia; Capitalising on the explosive growth" hopes to explain to visiting fund managers the potential benefits of investing in and setting up funds in Indonesia.

"Because of changes, including the liberalisation of capital markets in mutual funds, Indonesia is trying to promote domestic mutual funds and opening up to foreigners and fund managers," said conference organiser Fathi Fadzil of IBC Asia Ltd.
With a population of 193 million, resource-rich Indonesia is the world's fourth most populous nation behind China, India and the United States.
Indonesia's per capita income was US$993 in 1995, just below the US$1,000 level considered by the World Bank to be a springboard for the development of a burgeoning middle class.
Its economic promise has attracted attention and offers the potential for a domestic mutual funds industry.
Following regulatory changes last May, eight new mutual funds have been established holding 1.5 trillion rupiah, or about US$642 million, said Fadzil.
Mandatory retirement savings plans at all Indonesian corporations are expected to rapidly boost that figure, as well as the number of funds operating in the country.

"Most of the funds set up so far are pension funds. It's compulsory for all companies to set up pension funds for their employees, so these new funds provide another way of mobilising that money," Fadzil said.

The conference, which starts on Monday and lasts three days, kicks off with an explanation of recent regulatory changes designed to spur investment before launching into a variety of practical topics, such as how to market mutual funds in an Islamic region.
Islam is the main religion in Indonesia, with Moslems accounting for 87 percent of the population.
How to market and sell mutual funds throughout Southeast Asia as well as methods to define and assess risk in the region will also fall under the spotlight.

The conference organisers said a number of major international mutual funds had signed up, undeterred by the infant state of the nation's fund industry. Indeed, some speakers said the early stage of development was the primary reason they decided to participate.

"We're interested in it purely because we know the Indonesian mutual fund business and industry is very immature at the moment, but we know it's starting to develop and we want to learn more about what the local players are doing," said David O'Dwyer, general manager at industry monitoring group, Micropal Asia Ltd.
"The investment mangement business down there will be expanding rapidly. A lot of the international players are interested and it's a big potential market for this business."
